extracted.intended_audience: fiction writers and novelists studying point of view and dramatization
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for choosing and handling a limited point of view and for dramatizing a character's inner life so that thought is shown through surface images, scenes, and dialogue rather than by authorial exposition. Focuses on novel-length fiction where the principal interest is internal consciousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tell the story from the point of view that can best render the subject
rubrics_metrics.description: If the essential action of the story is a change in a man's vision or inner purpose, the story must be told from that man's point of view so the reader can share the gradations of his experience (e.g., Strether's change of purpose in The Ambassadors).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose a vantage that allows the reader to follow the long, slow internal process; an external or impersonal narrator will not convey the necessary subtlety of inner change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit the field of vision to a single consciousness when the subject is an impression
rubrics_metrics.description: When a tale 'consists entirely of an impression received by a certain man,' the narration should be bounded by that man's field of vision; the character cannot be fully rendered as an external figure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid presenting the character as seen from without; everything shown should be what the focal consciousness perceives, since outward behaviour often fails to express inner life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule out the ordinary dramatic method for primarily inward subjects
rubrics_metrics.description: If the story's centre is a moral or mental event within a character, the action-as-seen-from-outside (dramatic method) is inadequate and should be avoided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not try to 'stage' the internal event as external action; instead find ways to make internal processes visible through surface manifestations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dramatize the mind by presenting its surface images rather than by abstract exposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Make the working of a character's mind intelligible by showing the immediate 'flaw or ripple' of thought, successive images, and attendant scenes rather than providing retrospective accounts of inner events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arrange moments so that the reader 'sees' the thought as it passes across the mind; this permits suspense, gradual revelation, and the force of dramatic unfolding without explicit statement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Refrain from authorial intrusion and omniscient explanation
rubrics_metrics.description: Although the author knows the full truth of a character, he must 'carefully refrain from using his knowledge' so that the reader accepts nothing on authority and learns only by watching the presented images and scenes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author should 'vanish' like a playwright; avoid telling the reader what to think about a character's motives or providing wholesale summaries of inner states.

rubrics_metrics.name: Withhold full inner exposition; reveal by degrees to preserve dramatic effect
rubrics_metrics.description: A narrator who begins to expound a mind must tell all at once and thereby destroy suspense; withholding lets the story 'play out by due degrees' and preserves dramatic timing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use staged revelation—small glimpses, pauses, and restraint—so that secrets are inferred piecemeal rather than announced outright.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use scenes and dialogue as scenic substitution for narrative summary
rubrics_metrics.description: Conversations and dramatic scenes can put the reader 'in possession of all the past facts of the situation' without resorting to a clumsy lump of narrative; a scene can replace retrospective exposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design dialogue so it supplies necessary background and shapes the reader's knowledge organically, rather than dumping facts in narratorly summary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permit artful, unobtrusive shifts in point of view for reader advantage
rubrics_metrics.description: The author may subtly shift the point of view so that the reader sometimes occupies a better interpretive position than the focal character, but the shift must be 'insidious' and not betray the method.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shift only when it improves the reader's understanding and keep such moves so craftily arranged that they do not feel like authorial intrusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat description itself as dramatic material—animate the pictorial surface
rubrics_metrics.description: When the subject is non‑dramatic, heighten its pictorial description by applying 'the dramatic rule' to the elements of the picture so that description enacts the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't merely add more dialogue to make things lively; instead, make the descriptive elements behave like dramatic agents (images, light, gestures) that 'express the story in their behaviour.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Let characters in scenes sometimes appear objective while maintaining limited POV
rubrics_metrics.description: By keeping the focal consciousness's awareness in place but withholding access to its deeper thoughts during a scene, the character's speech and manner can seem to belong to an objectively observed person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame scenes within the focal vision but keep the mind out of sight—this creates the illusion of an independent figure and preserves dramatic immediacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use peripheral glimpses and multiple small views to give inner facts solidity
rubrics_metrics.description: Rather than stating inner facts directly, surround them with varied, often incidental glimpses (stereoscopically) so that the fact 'springs up complete and solid' in the reader's mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accumulate small, seemingly insignificant details and moments from different angles so the reader infers the deep facts, lending weight and three-dimensionality to what is concealed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid first-person/autobiographical narration when secrets must be guessed
rubrics_metrics.description: If a narrator were the principal actor (e.g., a murderer), admitting the reader to his mind would force full disclosure and ruin necessary guessing; first-person can destroy dramatic distance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select narrative stance that allows mystery to remain—use limited third-person or a dramatized consciousness rather than autobiographical confession when withholding is crucial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not use gratuitous dialogue that has nothing to contribute
rubrics_metrics.description: Peppering the surface with animated talk merely to increase liveliness cheapens conversation and undermines its force when genuine, essential talk is required later.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reserve dialogue for moments that contribute materially to the scene or to the dramatization of inner life; avoid filler talk that diminishes impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiply small dramatized moments rather than give a straight account
rubrics_metrics.description: To make a slow internal change apparent, present the mind 'at different moments, one after another'—brief scenes and glances that cumulatively reveal the silent change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer many brief enactments of thought over single summarizing statements; this 'roundabout' procedure produces the most direct impression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use dramatization to convert undramatic subjects into dramatic effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Even subjects that are pictorial and non-actional (e.g., Milly's inner condition) can be given the advantages of drama by making their superficial manifestations enact the deeper facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the same dramatizing methods (surface images, scenes, dialogue used dramatically) to build weight, authority, and presence for undramatic material.
